programs.sol:
"""A partial model of context-dependent lexical readings.

Fading function-word votes enable negative German verb beginnings and
passive 'worden', or negative Italian word pieces. Capitalized German
pieces get a weaker response. English 'time' distinguishes occasions
(next/each/last time, once upon a time) from durations (long/some time).
Kana context enables five Japanese lexical rules, especially deki (出来)
and kokochi (心地). Repeated middle-dot pieces have a negative response.
Other Japanese character-specific effects are deliberately left out,
rather than represented by a large token lookup table.
"""

import regex

READS = ()
GERMAN = set('''der die das den dem des und ist sind nicht auch für mit
auf zu im von ein eine einer einem einen sich als wird wurde werden
hat haben sein seine sie es er wir ich du aber nur nach bei aus daß
dass noch zum zur kann war waren soll sollte können würde hier diese
dieser dieses nun ohne doch so'''.split())
OTHER_FUNCTION_WORDS = set('''the and of to is that it for with this
was you are not on be at have or by an from he we they will but his her has can which
a i et les du dans au aux une pour avec est pas mais sur el los las
que por sin het een van zijn hij niet ook voor met maar'''.split())
ITALIAN = set('''di che il lo gli della delle degli nel nella alla sono
è dalla dello'''.split())
KANA = regex.compile(r'[\p{Hiragana}\p{Katakana}]')


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        carry = (doc, 0., 0., 0., 0., '', '')
    _, de, other, it, ja, last, tail = carry
    german = min(1., max(0., (de - other - it - .3) / 1.5))
    italian = min(1., max(0., (it - other - de - .3) / 1.5))
    japanese = min(1., ja)
    raw = s.strip()
    word = raw.lower()
    p = 0.

    if s.startswith(' ') and raw:
        # Short pieces of German be-/ge-/ent-/ver-/an- words.
        if word == 'worden':
            p = -11.5
        elif word == 'ent':
            p = -5.8
        elif word == 'ge':
            p = -4.5
        elif word == 'gen':
            p = -10. if last == 'so' else -6.
        elif word == 'gew':
            p = -3.
        elif word == 'be':
            p = -5.
        elif word in {'bes', 'bet', 'bez', 'beg', 'bed', 'beh'}:
            p = -1.4
        elif word == 'best':
            p = -2.5
        elif word in {'get', 'ger', 'gee'}:
            p = -2.2
        elif word in {'ver', 'verb', 'verd', 'verm'}:
            p = -1.4
        elif word in {'ang', 'ange', 'ans', 'ann', 'anz'}:
            p = -2.
        elif word in {'sol', 'hand'}:
            p = -4.5
        elif word == 'will':
            p = -4.8
        p *= german * (.25 if raw[0].isupper() else 1.)
        if word in {'col', 'sol', 'coin', 'cost', 'fin'}:
            p -= 5.8 * italian
        elif word in {'dis', 'ind', 'ins', 'int', 'inf', 'div',
                      'app', 'att', 'ass'}:
            p -= 1.8 * italian

        if word == 'time':
            p = {'next': 7.5, 'last': 3.5, 'each': 3., 'every': 1.4,
                 'another': 3., 'long': -2., 'some': -.8,
                 'hard': -1.2, 'this': .5, 'that': .3}.get(last, .05)
            if last == 'a':
                p = 7.8 if tail.rstrip().endswith('upon a') else .8
            if tail.endswith(('This', 'That')):
                p = 2.
        elif word == 'will':
            p += .1 * (1. - german)
    if s == 'age' and tail.endswith('d'):
        p = -4.5 * german  # the middle of German 'dagegen'

    if s == '出来':                    # deki: capability/completion
        p = -6.3 * japanese
    elif s == '地':                    # kokochi: comfort; other -chi words
        p = (-8. if tail.endswith('心') else -2.7) * japanese
    elif s == '解':                    # kai: explanation/solution
        p = -4. * japanese
    elif s == '体':                    # tai/karada: body
        p = 2.5 * japanese
    elif s == '中':                    # naka/chuu: inside/during
        p = 2.1 * japanese
    if s and all(c == '·' for c in s) and len(s) > 1:
        p = -2.4 if not tail or tail.endswith('·') else 0.

    # Vote only at word boundaries, not on suffixes of longer words.
    boundary = s.startswith(' ') or not tail or tail[-1].isspace()
    de = .97 * de + (boundary and word in GERMAN)
    other = .97 * other + (boundary and word in OTHER_FUNCTION_WORDS)
    it = .97 * it + (boundary and word in ITALIAN)
    ja = .9 * ja + bool(KANA.search(s))
    if s in {'<|endoftext|>', '<|im_start|>'}:
        de = other = it = ja = 0.
    return (doc, de, other, it, ja, word, (tail + s)[-40:]), float(p)

"""Draft 3: German/Italian word-start fragments, pushed negative.

In German or Italian text, the first piece of a word that the tokenizer split in two
(ent|standen, be|zeichnet, ge|bracht, sol|che, gew|esen, col|...) gets a strongly negative
activation; the more common, weaker fragments get smaller values. The same fragments in
English text (or code) do nothing, so the program first checks the last 30 tokens of the
same document: at least three German/Italian function words and at most one English one. A run of
middle-dot filler characters (·) also gets a fixed negative value.
"""
READS = ()

GERMAN_ITALIAN = frozenset(
    "und der die das ist nicht mit ein eine zu den sich auch wird von für dem im auf sie er "
    "es als bei nach oder aber sind wir ich werden hat noch wie di che il è della per una "
    "sono non anche gli delle come nel le un del al dei sul questo più ma si con da alla".split()
)
ENGLISH = frozenset(
    "the and of that with for are was this from have they their you your which would been "
    "there what about".split()
)
# Word-start fragments (the leading space is part of the token) and their typical activation.
FRAGMENTS = {
    "worden": -10.0, "ent": -6.0, "gen": -5.0, "will": -5.0, "be": -4.5, "ge": -4.5,
    "sol": -4.5, "col": -4.0, "gew": -3.0, "ang": -3.0, "div": -3.0, "fin": -2.5,
    "best": -2.0, "int": -2.0, "ins": -1.5, "ver": -1.2,
}
DOT_FILLER = "·"
DOT_VALUE = -2.4


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if token and set(token) == {DOT_FILLER}:
        return carry, DOT_VALUE
    if not (token.startswith(" ") and token[1:] in FRAGMENTS):
        return carry, 0.0
    # Look back over the last 30 tokens of this document only.
    current = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    recent = [
        s.strip().lower()
        for s, d in zip(prefix.token_strings[-30:], prefix.document_ids[-30:])
        if d == current
    ]
    german_italian = sum(w in GERMAN_ITALIAN for w in recent)
    english = sum(w in ENGLISH for w in recent)
    if german_italian >= 3 and english <= 1:
        return carry, FRAGMENTS[token[1:]]
    return carry, 0.0

programs.sol:
"""A document-initial spelling and word-class signal.

Most later tokens get zero. At the beginning, vowel counts and English
word classes supply a small additive score: activities/groups tend positive,
while evaluative qualities and adverbs tend negative. Repeating the initial
token keeps its score; the first different token ends that initial regime.
Whitespace and punctuation get simple offsets, with decorative dot/caret
runs handled explicitly. This is a coarse predictor, not a dictionary of
token activations.
"""
from functools import lru_cache
import wordnet
from wordfreq import zipf_frequency

READS = ()

# English grammatical classes and descriptive/evaluative vocabulary.
WORD_CLASSES = (
    # desirable or standard qualities
    (-4.72,
     'amazing appropriate awesome beautiful brilliant easy effective '
     'efficient essential excellent fantastic free fresh good gratis great '
     'happy healthy helpful ideal important impressive lovely natural '
     'necessary nice normal perfect regular remarkable standard suitable '
     'superb superior typical useful usual valuable wonderful'),

    # newness
    (-2.92, 'latest modern new recent'),

    # modal
    (2.49, 'can could may might must ought shall should will would'),

    # have
    (2.56, 'had has have having'),

    # pronoun
    (0.57,
     'he her hers him his i me mine my our ours she their theirs them they '
     'us we you your yours'),

    # conjunction
    (-1.72, 'and but nor or so yet'),

    # preposition
    (-0.81,
     'after among as at before between by for from in into of on onto over '
     'through to under with within without'),

    # comparison
    (-1.32,
     'alternative alternatively another different else instead other same '
     'similar such unlike'),

    # quantity
    (-2.33,
     'all any both each either enough every few least less many more most '
     'much several some'),

)
WORD_CLASSES = [(weight, frozenset(words.split()))
                for weight, words in WORD_CLASSES]

# WordNet lexicographer categories. A word can belong to several.
SEMANTICS = {
    'verb.motion': 0.92,
    'adv.all': -0.82,
    'noun.group': 1.11,
    'verb.competition': 1.5,
    'noun.substance': -0.85,
    'noun.event': 1.06,
    'verb.cognition': 0.74,
    'noun.person': 0.53,
    'noun.attribute': -0.92,
    'noun.communication': 0.3,
    'noun.Tops': 1.82,  # General entity/object vocabulary.
    'noun.relation': -0.73,
    'noun.act': 0.42,
    'noun.state': 0.28,
}

VOWELS = {
    'a': -0.53,
    'e': -0.77,
    'i': 1.74,
    'o': 0.43,
    'y': 0.83,
}

SUFFIXES = {
    'ing': -1.4,
    'ly': -2.29,
    'al': -1.02,
    'tion': -1.17,
}


@lru_cache(maxsize=8192)
def initial_score(text):
    s = text.strip()
    word = s.lower()
    # Decorative dot/caret runs are a conspicuous special case.
    if s and not s.strip("·"):
        return 6.0
    if len(s) > 1 and not s.strip("^"):
        return 4.9

    value = 1.08
    if not s:
        value -= 1.8
    if "\t" in text:
        value += 3.95
    if text.startswith(" "):
        value += 0.53
    if s.isdigit():
        value -= 1.6
    if s and not any(c.isalnum() for c in s):
        value -= 1.04
    if s.istitle():
        value += 0.34
    if not (word.isascii() and word.isalpha()):
        return value
    forms = set(wordnet.base_forms(word)) | {word}
    for weight, words in WORD_CLASSES:
        if forms & words:
            value += weight
    value += sum(weight * word.count(c) for c, weight in VOWELS.items())
    value += sum(SEMANTICS.get(c, 0.0) for c in wordnet.categories(word))
    for suffix, weight in SUFFIXES.items():
        if len(word) > len(suffix) + 2 and word.endswith(suffix):
            value += weight
    if zipf_frequency(word, "en") >= 6:
        value -= 1.0
    return value


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    document = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    token = prefix.token_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or document != carry[0]:
        value = initial_score(prefix.token_strings[-1])
        return (document, token, value, True), float(value)
    doc, first_token, value, initial = carry
    initial = initial and token == first_token
    return (doc, first_token, value, initial), float(value if initial else 0.0)

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:833 -- a document-opening detector with a word-class sign.

The component is silent inside a document. Its activation is large only at a
document's first token: position 0 of a row, or any token right after
<|endoftext|>. There the value depends on which word it is. Plain English
words get a positive value, adjectives, adverbs and determiners/quantifiers
(words that open a modifier phrase) a negative one, and punctuation, code and
CJK tokens sit in between.

This program reproduces that with three calibrated group means. It captures
only the coarse word-class sign; the real per-word values vary widely.
"""

READS = ()
EOT = "<|endoftext|>"

# Words that open a modifier phrase: determiners, quantifiers, adverbs, common adjectives.
MODIFIERS = set(
    """great best most more some new latest green red free still always especially
    extremely essentially necessarily minimal amazing perpendicular enough currently
    also now and other many several few all any each every both much very really just
    only even often never ever already the a an this that these those my your his her
    its our their""".split()
)

WORD_VALUE = 2.0       # plain English word at a document start
MODIFIER_VALUE = -3.0  # modifier / determiner / -ly adverb at a document start
OTHER_VALUE = 0.9      # punctuation, digits, code, CJK, other scripts


def word_class(text):
    word = text.strip()
    if not word or not word.isascii() or not word[0].isalpha():
        return "other"
    lower = word.lower()
    if lower in MODIFIERS or (lower.endswith("ly") and len(lower) > 4):
        return "modifier"
    return "word"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    opens_document = t == 0 or prefix.token_strings[t - 1] == EOT
    if not opens_document:
        return None, 0.0
    value = {"word": WORD_VALUE, "modifier": MODIFIER_VALUE, "other": OTHER_VALUE}
    return None, value[word_class(prefix.token_strings[t])]

programs.sol:
"""Negative responses to writing fragments, not to a general writing topic.

Detect 写/寫 (also used in Japanese 写真) and Slavic pis/píš, пис/пиш.
Split roots respond strongly; merged prefixes/suffixes weaken the signal.
Recent kana strengthens 写/寫, and a short trace covers following suffixes.
Proper names, acronyms, and non-writing inflections are downweighted.
Other, unrelated component responses are deliberately left at zero.
"""
import codecs
import re
import unicodedata

READS = ()
ROOT = re.compile(r'pis|piš|пи[сш]')
SLAVIC_PREFIXES = {
    '', 'o', 'u', 's', 'w', 'wy', 'z', 'za', 'na', 'do', 'od',
    'po', 'pod', 'prze', 'przy', 'pre', 'pře', 'při', 'pro', 'roz', 'vy',
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        carry = (doc, b'', '', 100, 0.0)
    _, pending, word, kana_age, trace = carry
    raw = pending + prefix.token_bytes[-1]
    text, used = codecs.utf_8_decode(raw, 'ignore', False)
    pending = raw[used:]
    names = (unicodedata.name(c, '') for c in text)
    kana_age = 0 if any('HIRAGANA' in n or 'KATAKANA' in n
                        for n in names) else kana_age + 1
    token = text.lower().replace('í', 'i')
    continues = bool(token and token[0].isalpha())
    old_length = len(word) if continues else 0
    for char in token:
        word = word + char if char.isalpha() else ''
    word = word[-64:]
    value = trace if continues else 0.0
    next_trace = trace * 0.2 if continues else 0.0
    clean = text.strip()
    if clean in ('写', '寫'):
        value = -5.6 - 2.3 * (kana_age < 32)
        next_trace = 0.0
    elif any(c in clean for c in '写寫'):
        value = -1.8 / max(1, len(clean) - 1)
        next_trace = 0.0

    matches = list(ROOT.finditer(word))
    if matches and matches[-1].end() > old_length:
        root = matches[-1]
        cyrillic = root.group().startswith('п')
        prefix_text, suffix = word[:root.start()], word[root.end():]
        if cyrillic or prefix_text in SLAVIC_PREFIXES:
            scale = 0.8 ** len(suffix)
            if cyrillic:
                split = root.start() < old_length
                base = -10.5 if root.group().endswith('ш') else -8.0
                if not split:
                    base = -4.0
                    scale *= 0.75 ** max(0, root.start() - old_length)
                if suffix.startswith('т'):
                    scale *= 0.3
            else:
                base = -7.5 if prefix_text else -3.5
                if not prefix_text and text.strip()[:1].isupper():
                    scale *= 0.1
                if text.isupper() and len(text) >= 3:
                    scale *= 0.05
                if suffix.startswith(('o', 't', 'c')):
                    scale *= 0.15
            value = base * scale
            next_trace = value * 0.25
    return (doc, pending, word, kana_age, next_trace), float(value)
programs.haiku:
"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:834 -- a "write" detector.

The component goes strongly negative on the piece of a token that completes the
word-stem for "write": the Russian/Polish/Czech stem пис- / пиш- (писать, написать,
напиши, опишите, писатель, pisać, napisz) and the Chinese character 写 / 寫 (写作, 写真).
It is negative because the model is reading a word meaning "write". The strongest
responses are on the short stem-ending pieces (ис, ши, ш, иш, Latin "is" after "p"/"op"),
about -7 to -13; the bare piece "пис" and Chinese 写 are about -4 to -6; the endings
after the stem (ать, ал, ания) are weaker, around -1.5. Other places, including most
text, give 0. Positive activations (up to +5, e.g. in поперечное, непри-ятный) are
not modelled: they are diffuse.

Rules, in order, on the current token and the word typed so far:
  - 写 or 寫 on its own: -6.
  - a character 写 inside a longer token: -3.
  - the word so far (letters only, reset by spaces and punctuation) gains the stem:
    -7 if this token is 1-2 letters (the ending that completes пис/пиш), else -2.
  - the stem was already in the word: -1.5 for the endings after it.
  - a word ending in "пи" (the start of пиш-/пис-): -2.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# пис / пиш, or Latin pis, but not the 'list' word список or the English 'APIs'
STEM = re.compile(r"(?<!с)пис|пиш|(?<!e)(?<!ap)pis(?!to|ton|t)")
PARTIAL = re.compile(r"пи$")
CHINESE_WRITE = re.compile(r"写|寫")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    word = "" if carry is None or carry[0] != doc else carry[1]
    raw = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    piece = raw.strip().lower()
    value = 0.0
    if piece in {"写", "寫"}:
        value = -6.0
        word = ""
    elif CHINESE_WRITE.search(piece):
        value = -3.0
        word = ""
    elif piece.isalpha():
        if raw[:1].isspace():
            word = ""
        cur = word + piece
        if STEM.search(cur):
            if STEM.search(word):
                value = -1.5
            else:
                value = -7.0 if len(piece) <= 2 else -2.0
        elif PARTIAL.search(cur):
            value = -2.0
        word = cur
    else:
        word = ""
    return (doc, word), value

"""Layer 1, MLP down-projection, component 835: a Greek-script detector.

In plain terms: this component is near zero on almost all text, and goes negative
where Greek letters are being decoded from split or broken bytes:

1. Polytonic Greek letters (U+1F00-U+1FFF: letters with breathing marks, accents and
   iota subscripts, as in ancient Greek) are the strongest trigger, about -0.9. A
   polytonic letter right after a broken-byte fragment (U+FFFD) is more negative.
2. A plain Greek letter right after a broken-byte fragment is strongly negative, about
   -0.7 on average (it is often the letter that follows a garbled run).
3. Otherwise, plain Greek letters (without a leading space) and bare fragments are
   weakly negative, more so the more Greek or broken text is in the last few tokens.
4. The capital "O" that opens "OBSERVATION:" right after a tool-response tag is about
   -0.7.

Everywhere else (ASCII, CJK, Cyrillic, ...) it predicts 0. The numbers are the
least-squares fit on 4096 training rows, rounded.

The program keeps the last RECENT tokens of each document, to measure how much Greek
or broken text is nearby, and to see whether the token before was a fragment.
Document boundaries reset it.
"""

READS = ()

RECENT = 8  # earlier tokens that count as nearby
MAX_DENSITY = 4

TOOL_HEADER_O = -0.7  # "O" of "OBSERVATION:" after <tool_response>
POLYTONIC = -0.9  # a token holding a polytonic Greek letter
POLYTONIC_AFTER_FRAGMENT = -0.25  # extra, if the token before is a fragment
GREEK_AFTER_FRAGMENT = -0.7  # a plain Greek letter right after a fragment
GREEK_PER_NEARBY = -0.04  # per nearby Greek-or-fragment token
FRAGMENT_PER_NEARBY = -0.05  # per nearby Greek-or-fragment token, for a bare fragment


def is_greek(ch):
    return "Ͱ" <= ch <= "Ͽ" or "ἀ" <= ch <= "῿"


def is_polytonic(text):
    return any("ἀ" <= ch <= "῿" for ch in text)


def greekish(text):
    return "�" in text or any(is_greek(ch) for ch in text)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_row = len(prefix) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    history = () if new_row or carry is None else tuple(carry)
    before = history[-1] if history else ""
    nearby = min(MAX_DENSITY, sum(greekish(s) for s in history[-RECENT:]))
    after_fragment = before == "�"

    value = 0.0
    if text == "O" and before == "\n" and "<tool_response>" in "".join(history[-4:]):
        value = TOOL_HEADER_O
    elif is_polytonic(text):
        value = POLYTONIC + (POLYTONIC_AFTER_FRAGMENT if after_fragment else 0.0)
    elif text == "�":
        value = FRAGMENT_PER_NEARBY * nearby
    elif any(is_greek(ch) for ch in text) and not text.startswith(" "):
        value = GREEK_AFTER_FRAGMENT if after_fragment else GREEK_PER_NEARBY * nearby

    return (history + (text,))[-RECENT:], value

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:836 -- a "word-start syllable" detector (negative).

The component goes negative on two-letter consonant-vowel pieces such as "Ra", "Be",
"ge", "ko", "Ha", "Sa": short syllables that begin a longer word in a language that
is not English (German "Be|iträge", "ge|ändert", Russian "по", Cyrillic "ко").
Common English two-letter words ("He", "To", "We", "So", "My", "be") and all-caps
pieces stay near zero. The strongest responses are title-case pieces that start a
word, after a space or punctuation. A piece that continues a word after a letter
(mid-word) responds only weakly. Other tokens predict 0.

The program needs no state: it reads the newest token and the one before it.
"""

READS = ()

VOWELS = set("aeiouyäöüéèàáíóúаеёиоуыэюяɛə")
# Common English two-letter words that look like consonant-vowel syllables.
ENGLISH_WORDS = set(
    "be he me we so to do go no by my or of on in at is it if an as us ok hi oh am".split()
)


def is_cv_syllable(core):
    """Two letters: one consonant then one vowel, not an English word."""
    if len(core) != 2 or not core.isalpha():
        return False
    first, second = core[0].lower(), core[1].lower()
    return first not in VOWELS and second in VOWELS and core.lower() not in ENGLISH_WORDS


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    core = token.strip()
    if not is_cv_syllable(core):
        return carry, 0.0
    # The piece starts a word if it has a leading space, follows punctuation,
    # opens the document, or follows a token that is not a letter.
    previous = prefix.token_strings[-2] if len(prefix) > 1 else ""
    same_doc = len(prefix) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    starts_word = token[:1].isspace() or not same_doc or not previous[-1:].isalpha()
    if not starts_word:
        return carry, -0.13
    # Title case ("Ra", "Be") responds more than lowercase ("ge", "ko").
    title = core[0].isupper() and core[1:].islower()
    return carry, -1.3 if title else -0.6

programs.sol:
"""A document-initial lexical response.

Large activations in the training examples occurred on the first token of a
row or document; later values were small. Predict zero after that first token.
At the start, approximate the lexical response using a few literal word
families, closed grammatical classes, and character shape. These are average
responses, not a claim that every member of a semantic class behaves alike.
Substantial individual-word variation is deliberately left unexplained.
"""
import unicodedata
import regex
import wordnet

READS = ()

# Responses for a digit at the start, in numerical order.
DIGITS = (-0.87, -2.55, -1.07, -0.68, -0.22,
          0.53, -0.63, -1.24, 0.29, -1.19)

# Initial punctuation, allowing adjoining whitespace/newlines.
PUNCTUATION = {

  the token right after an <|endoftext|> marker. There the activation is set by the token

  "2" gets about 3.2.

SPIKE = 3.2  # "2" directly after a text-initial "1"

"""A closing-code-block detector, not a generic right-brace detector.

Most tokens get zero. Bare braces ending statements or indented code blocks
get positive values; inline data and mathematical braces are much weaker.
The estimate adjusts for indentation, line-numbered source, printed escapes,
and Markdown code markers. Empty function bodies are also positive.
A following spaced code marker or line break can retain some of the signal.
These are local formatting heuristics, not a full code parser.
"""
import re

READS = ()


def predict(token, history):
    body = token.lstrip(' \t')
    previous = history[-1] if history else ''
    if body == '··':
        return -1.7  # Paired middle dots are a separate negative punctuation cue.
    if re.fullmatch(r'[();]*;\}\s*', body):
        return 4.0
    if re.fullmatch(r'[()]+\{\}\s*', body):
        return 6.3
    if body.startswith('{}'):
        kind = 'empty'
    elif body.startswith('}'):
        tail = body[1:]
        if not tail.strip():
            kind = 'plain'
        elif tail.startswith(('\\', '`', 'else', 'catch', 'finally')):
            kind = 'plain'
        elif tail.startswith(','):
            kind = 'comma'
        elif tail.startswith(')'):
            kind = 'paren'
        elif tail.startswith(';'):
            kind = 'semicolon'
        elif tail.startswith('}'):
            kind = 'double'
        else:
            return 0.0
    elif body.strip() and set(body.strip()) <= set('^~'):
        indented = previous.isspace() and len(previous) > 2
        if set(body.strip()) == {'^'}:
            return 0.05 + 2.2 * indented + ('\n' in token)
        if set(body.strip()) == {'~'}:
            return 0.2 + 2.3 * indented
        return 0.0
    else:
        return 0.0

        if not body[1:].strip():
            return 1.4 if '\n' in token else -2.7
        return -1.0

    text = ''.join(history)
    text = re.sub(r'\\+r?\\+n|\\+n|\\+r', '\n', text)
    text = re.sub(r'\\+t', '\t', text)
    line = text.rsplit('\n', 1)[-1]
    numbered = bool(re.match(r'^ *\d+(?:\t|[-:])', line))
    text = re.sub(r'(?m)^ *\d+(?:\t|[-:])', '', text)
    text = re.sub(r'(?m)^[+-]', '', text)
    text = re.sub(r'(?m)^\s*// ?', '', text)
    line = text.rsplit('\n', 1)[-1]
    own_line = not line.strip()
    prior = text.rstrip(' \t\r\n`\xa0')
    last = prior[-1:] or ' '

    if kind != 'plain':
        value = {'empty': 0.55, 'comma': 0.0, 'paren': 0.1,
                 'semicolon': -0.35, 'double': -0.35}[kind]
        value += 0.7 * own_line - 1.05 * numbered
        value += 1.35 * (last == ';') + 0.35 * (last == '{')
        if kind == 'empty' and (last == ')' or prior.endswith('=>')):

        return value

    value += own_line * (2.45 + 0.06 * min(indent, 24))
    value -= 0.95 * numbered
    value += {';': 2.3, '{': 1.8, '}': 0.2, ',': -0.4,

    value -= 0.25 * last.isalnum()
    value += 2.1 * (last == ';' and not own_line)
    value += 0.8 * bool(re.search(r'\breturn\b[^\n;]*$', prior))
    value -= 0.65 * bool(re.search(r'[:,][^;{}\n]*$', prior))
    value -= 0.55 * (previous.isspace() and '\t' in previous and ' ' in previous)
    value += 1.75 * (bool(previous.strip()) and set(previous.strip()) == {'`'})
    value += 0.6 * body[1:].startswith('`')
    value -= 0.3 * body[1:].startswith(('else', 'catch', 'finally'))
    return value

    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]

    '~': 0.27, '"': 0.30, "'": 0.30, 'other': 0.013,

Chinese and Japanese text normally uses full-width punctuation (，。：；？！）. This
component responds to a half-width mark such as a comma, period, colon, semicolon,
question mark, exclamation mark or closing parenthesis:

- strongly when the mark comes straight after a Chinese character or a kana
  (Han ideograph, hiragana, katakana), e.g. "重要," or "时间:";
- weakly when it comes after something else (a Latin word, a digit, a bracket)
  inside a stretch of mostly CJK text (at least 1 in 5 of the last 24 tokens CJK);
- about zero everywhere else, including full-width marks (，。), Hangul, and
  ordinary English punctuation.

The strengths are the typical activations for each mark, read off training text.
"""

# typical activation of each half-width mark straight after CJK text
STRENGTH = {",": 2.7, ".": 3.0, ":": 3.0, ";": 2.1, "?": 2.3, "!": 2.2, ")": 1.1}
WEAK = 0.6  # the same marks after non-CJK text inside mostly-CJK text
WINDOW = 24  # how many earlier tokens of the same document to look at


def is_cjk(s):
    """True if the token's last character is a Han ideograph or a kana."""
    if not s:
        return False
    ch = s[-1]
    return "぀" <= ch <= "ヿ" or "㐀" <= ch <= "鿿"

    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if tok not in STRENGTH or len(prefix) < 2:
        return None, 0.0

    docs = prefix.document_ids
    lo = max(0, len(prefix) - 1 - WINDOW)
    before = [prefix.token_strings[q] for q in range(lo, len(prefix) - 1) if docs[q] == docs[-1]]
    if not before:
        return None, 0.0
    if is_cjk(before[-1]):
        return None, STRENGTH[tok]

    return None, WEAK if share >= 0.2 else 0.0

What the component does: it is a "sweet" detector. On the token that completes the word
"sweet" (sweet, Sweet, sweets, sweeter, sweetness, bittersweet) it pushes strongly negative,

few words (walk, ski, watch, wick) get a small positive one. Everything else is 0.

The program tracks the letters of the current word across tokens (resetting at each new
document and at any non-letter), and fires on the token that first spells the root.

READS = ()

SWEET_ROOTS = ("sweet", "tweet")
SOUND_ALIKES = ("awesome", "wheat", "sweat", "weiß")
POSITIVE_WORDS = ("ski", "walk", "watch", "wick")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc, word = carry if carry else (None, "")
    if prefix.document_ids[-1] != doc:  # a new document starts a new word
        word = ""
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    piece = prefix.token_strings[-1]

    before = word  # letters of the word before this token
    for ch in piece:
        word = word + ch.lower() if ch.isalpha() else ""

    def first(root):  # this token is where the root first appears in the word

    elif first("tweet"):

    elif word.endswith(("swe", "twe")) and not any(r in before for r in SWEET_ROOTS):

    elif piece.lower() == "we" and before:  # a fragment inside a word
        value = -5.0 if before.endswith(("s", "t", "z", "ch")) else -1.0
    elif any(first(w) for w in SOUND_ALIKES):
        value = -1.5
    elif piece in POSITIVE_WORDS:

    else:

It is silent on almost every token. It responds to three things:

- The Chinese character 言 (speech, words) and its Korean reading 언 (as in 선언):
  positive, about +2 (observed +0.5 to +3.4).
- The math symbols for the Greek letters phi and xi, written in Latin letters
  ("Phi", "phi", "xi", "Xi"): weakly negative, about -1 (observed -0.6 to -0.9).

rule on all Greek letters (or on German/Dutch-style word endings like "-er",

Context is not used, so the program is stateless.
"""

READS = ()

PSI = {"psi", "ψ", "Psi", "Ψ"}
SPEECH = {"言", "언"}
MATH_GREEK_NAMES = {"Phi", "phi", "xi", "Xi"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Return this position's predicted activation for the current token."""
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:850: a sparse, mostly silent feature in layer 1's MLP.

What the program predicts, in plain terms:

1. Document starts (the only effect that matters much). The first token of each
   document, the token after <|endoftext|> or the first token of a row, has an
   activation that is a fixed function of that token alone (no context: attention
   resets at a document start). It is negative for most words and punctuation
   (about -0.2), slightly positive for digits (+0.09), and near zero for bare
   spaces. The program uses these averages by token type.

2. Compound heads (weak, mostly unexplained). The feature can be strongly positive
   (1-3) on the second word of a two-word term whose first word is a modifier,
   such as "cell|phone", "atomic|bomb", "public|library", "young|people",
   "secondary|battery", or the Chinese 公|債 and 電動|車. Which pairs fire depends on
   the specific words, and a rule over word classes is too imprecise: on average
   a head after an adjective-like word is only about +0.01. The program gives that
   small average, nothing more.

Everything else is predicted as 0. The program keeps no state across positions.
"""

READS = ()

# Common function words: a modifier before a head must be a content word.
FUNCTION_WORDS = frozenset(
    """a an the of in on at to for from by with and or but as is are was were be been
    it its this that these those he she they we you i his her their our your my me him
    them us not no so if than then there here which who what when where why how all any
    can will would should could may might must do does did have has had also into over
    under about between after before during while up down out more most other only
    own same too very just""".split()
)

ADJECTIVE_LIKE = re.compile(r"(al|ic|ous|ive|ary|ent|ful|able|ian|ial|ular|ed|ish)$")

CJK = re.compile(r"[一-鿿]")

# Constants: what the feature averages in each situation, measured on training text.
COMPOUND_HEAD = 0.008  # English head word after an adjective-like content word
CJK_COMPOUND = 0.008  # second CJK character after a CJK character


def first_token_value(s):
    """Activation on the first token of a document: a function of the token alone."""
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s?\d+", s):
        return 0.09  # digits
    if CJK.search(s):
        return -0.24
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s?[A-Z][a-z]+", s):
        return -0.19  # capitalised word
    if re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]+", s):
        return -0.20  # lowercase word, no leading space
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s[a-z]+", s):
        return -0.07  # lowercase word after a space
    if s.strip() == "":
        return 0.0
    return -0.16  # punctuation and symbols


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    cur = prefix.token_strings[t]
    if t == 0 or docs[t] != docs[t - 1]:
        return carry, first_token_value(cur)
    prev = prefix.token_strings[t - 1]
    prev_word = prev.strip().lower()
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s[A-Za-z]+", cur) and cur.strip().lower() not in FUNCTION_WORDS:
        if re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]+", prev_word) and prev_word not in FUNCTION_WORDS:
            if ADJECTIVE_LIKE.search(prev_word):
                return carry, COMPOUND_HEAD
    if CJK.search(cur) and CJK.search(prev):
        return carry, CJK_COMPOUND
    return carry, 0.0

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:852: the "string piece glued on by + or <<" detector.

What it does
    This component goes strongly negative on the opening quote of a string literal
    that is appended to code with a concatenation operator:

        "Processing " + this.files.length + " files"     Java/JS/Python: +
        cout << "Worker " << worker << " assigned"        C++ streams: <<
        $x . "\n"                                         PHP: .

    The size depends on what the piece is glued onto. After a closing paren, as in
    `size() + "`, it is about -7. After a bare name, as in `x + "`, it is about -3.5.
    After `<<` it is about -2.5.

    Two smaller effects are included:
      * a `}` that closes a `{name}` or `${name}` placeholder inside a double-quoted
        string (about -2) or a backtick template (about -3);
      * the first token of each new document (about +0.25).

    Every other token is predicted as 0. Most of the component's variance is a
    diffuse, near-zero background (std about 0.07 per token) that no short rule
    captures. This program explains about a quarter of the variance on eval rows
    (0.24) and about 0.21 on a larger local sample. It gets the large concatenation
    events right, and those dominate the squared activation.

Why
    When a language builds a string in code, the model has to start a new literal
    after an operator. This component writes the "I am inside a glued-on string
    piece" signal into the residual stream, with a size that depends on what the
    piece is attached to.

How it runs
    `step` is called once per token. It keeps a small carry: whether it is inside a
    double-quoted or backtick string on the current line, the text since the last
    opening brace, the previous token, and the character that ended the token
    before it. Only the prefix is read, so the program is causal.
"""

READS = ()

QUOTES = ('"', "'", "`")
NAME_CHARS = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789_ .-")


def is_placeholder_close(carry):
    """True if the text since the last '{' or '[' on this line is a bare name and we are
    inside a double-quoted string or a backtick template."""
    tail = carry["tail"]
    return bool(tail) and set(tail) <= NAME_CHARS and (carry["dq"] or carry["bt"])


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # Start of a document: reset the carry (a row can hold several documents).
    new_doc = (
        carry is None
        or prefix.position == 0
        or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    )
    if carry is None or prefix.position == 0:
        carry = {"dq": False, "bt": False, "tail": None, "prev": "", "before": ""}

    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    body = cur.lstrip()
    prev = carry["prev"]        # the token before this one
    before = carry["before"]    # last character of the token before the operator

    value = 0.0
    if body.startswith(("<<", "+")) and len(body) > 2 and body[-1:] in QUOTES:
        value = -2.5            # operator and opening quote in one token, e.g. +"
    elif body[:1] in QUOTES and (prev.endswith("+") or prev.endswith(" .")):
        value = -7.0 if before == ")" else -3.5   # string piece glued on by + or .
    elif body[:1] in QUOTES and prev.endswith("<<"):
        value = -2.5            # string piece streamed on by <<
    elif body[:1] == "}" and is_placeholder_close(carry):
        value = -3.0 if carry["bt"] else -2.0   # closes {name} inside a string or template
    elif new_doc and prefix.position > 0:
        value = 0.25            # first token of a new document

    # Update the carry with this token's characters.
    dq, bt, tail = carry["dq"], carry["bt"], carry["tail"]
    for ch in cur:
        if ch == "\n":
            dq = bt = False
            tail = None
        elif ch == '"' and not bt:
            dq = not dq
        elif ch == "`" and not dq:
            bt = not bt
        elif ch in "{[":
            tail = ""
        elif ch in "}]":
            tail = None
        elif tail is not None:
            tail += ch
    new_before = prev.rstrip()[-1:] if prev.strip() else before
    return {"dq": dq, "bt": bt, "tail": tail, "prev": cur.rstrip(), "before": new_before}, value

"""Layer 1, MLP down_proj, component 858: a 'return' or 'break' that opens a line, a few
other context rules, and near zero everywhere else.

What it responds to, as a person would describe it:
- Start of a document (the first token after <|endoftext|>, or the first token of a packed row):
  mildly positive, about +0.45 on average.
- A 'Title:' header at the start of a document: the colon is strongly negative (-10).
- 'return' or 'break' opening a line of code, after its indentation: negative. It is strongest
  one indent level deep (a function body: 4 spaces or one tab, about -1.7), weaker when nested
  deeper (about -0.3 at 0 or 5-8 columns), and absent at 9 or more columns.
- Indentation of 4 or more columns after a newline: slightly positive (+0.15).
- A long run of doubled middle dots '··' (leader lines): about +0.95, as observed in one all-dot row.
Everything else is predicted as 0. Tokens are read in order; state carried between positions is
the position within the document, whether a line has started, the indentation width, and the
length of the current run of dots.
"""

READS = ()

DOC_START = 0.45        # first token of a document (or of a packed row)
TITLE_COLON = -10.0     # the ':' of 'Title:' when 'Title' opens a document
RETURN_BODY = -1.7      # 'return' / 'break' opening a line one indent level deep (4 spaces or a tab)
RETURN_OTHER = -0.3     # the same keywords at other indentation levels
INDENT = 0.15           # an indentation of 4 or more columns right after a newline
DOT_RUN = 0.95          # a '··' inside a run of 8 or more such tokens
DOT_TOKEN = "··"


def width(text):
    # indentation width in columns: a tab counts as 4
    return sum(4 if c == "\t" else 1 for c in text)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (tokens since document start, at a line start?, indentation columns, '··' run length)
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        since, line_start, indent, run = 0, True, 0, 0
    else:
        since, line_start, indent, run = carry[0] + 1, carry[1], carry[2], carry[3]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if since > 0 else ""
    run = run + 1 if s == DOT_TOKEN else 0
    core = s.lstrip(" \t")
    value = 0.0
    if since == 0:
        value = DOC_START
    elif since == 1 and s == ":" and prev == "Title":
        value = TITLE_COLON
    elif core.strip() in ("return", "break") and line_start:
        columns = indent + width(s[: len(s) - len(core)])
        value = RETURN_BODY if 1 <= columns <= 4 else (RETURN_OTHER if columns <= 8 else 0.0)
    elif run >= 8:
        value = DOT_RUN
    elif line_start and s.strip() == "" and width(s) >= 4:
        value = INDENT
    # track the line: a newline starts a line, whitespace before a token indents it
    if "\n" in s:
        line_start, indent = True, width(s.split("\n")[-1])
    elif s.strip() == "" and s != "":
        indent += width(s)
    else:
        line_start, indent = False, 0
    return (since, line_start, indent, run), value

"""Component layers.1.mlp.down_proj:859 -- the spelled "u then i" detector.

The component reads the letter pair "u" then "i" inside a word, spelled either
inside one token or split across a token boundary:
  - "Pituit" | "ary": the "ary" after "pituit" (pituitary) is its strongest case
  - a word-final u | i-token: "nu" | "isance", "Cru" | "ik", "Lu" | "igi", "ru" | "ir"
  - inside one token: "uit", "uid", "uis" (annuity, UID, nuisance, suit); bare
    "uit"/"uid"/"uis" tokens are strongest, longer words with them weaker
The "u" of "ou", "qu", "gu" (you, quit, guide) does not count, and neither do
i-words like "ill", "ion", "ice", "inea", or "ui" after b, c, f, g, l, o, q, r
(build, circuit, fluid, Louis, quit). A repeated middle-dot leader token ("··")
pushes it negative.

READS = ()

SPLIT_U = re.compile(r"(?<![oqg])u$", re.I)           # word-final u, not ou / qu / gu
I_START = re.compile(r"^i[srzkbgt]", re.I)             # token starts i + s/r/z/k/b/g/t
UI_TAIL = re.compile(r"(?<![bcfglorq])ui[tds]", re.I)  # uit, uid, uis
UI = re.compile(r"(?<![bcfglorq])ui", re.I)            # any other ui
BARE = {"uit", "uid", "uis", "uits", "uity"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if tok == "··":
        return carry, -3.0
    prev = ""
    if prefix.position > 0 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]:

    if tok.lower() == "ary" and prev.lower().endswith("uit"):

    if I_START.search(tok) and SPLIT_U.search(prev):
        return carry, 2.3                      # u | i-token across a boundary
    if UI_TAIL.search(tok):
        return carry, 3.1 if tok.lower() in BARE else 0.6
    if UI.search(tok):
        return carry, 0.5                      # other ui fragments
    return carry, 0.0

"""Candidate 4: nouns that take a preposition complement, versus measure nouns.

Some nouns are normally followed by a fixed preposition: "a sense of", "an idea of",
"an impact on", "a look at", "no interest in". Two places carry the signal:
  * the noun itself, after "a / an / no / any" (strongest after "have", "get", "give"):
    "have no idea", "have a look", "gives you a sense";
  * the preposition right after such a noun: "sense [of]", "impact [on]".

MENTAL = set("""idea ideas sense insight insights overview understanding view views perspective

talent appetite background introduction information info advice estimate expectations
impact impacts effect effects influence interest relevance regard control access role

MEASURE = set("""sum sums total aggregate average maximum minimum exact absolute typical final
product distance difference angle height depth area volume weight force power rate ratio
number value amount count limit fee penalty""".split())

INDEFINITE = {"a", "an", "no", "any", "some", "little", "better", "clear", "good", "direct",
              "significant"}
LIGHT_VERBS = {"have", "has", "had", "having", "get", "got", "give", "gave", "take", "took"}
PREPOSITIONS = {"of", "on", "to", "for", "in", "with", "at", "into", "over", "about"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tokens = [t.strip().lower() for t in prefix.token_strings[-5:]]
    word, before = tokens[-1], tokens[-2] if len(tokens) > 1 else ""
    if word in PREPOSITIONS and before in MENTAL:

    if word in PREPOSITIONS and before in MEASURE:
        return carry, -0.3
    if word in MENTAL and before in INDEFINITE:
        light = any(t in LIGHT_VERBS for t in tokens[:-2])
        return carry, 1.5 if light else 0.6
    if word in MEASURE and before in INDEFINITE:
        return carry, -0.3
    return carry, 0.0

    if t == 0 or d[t] != d[t - 1]:

    if s[t] != "." or not s[t - 1].isdigit():
        return None, 0.0
    # walk back over the digits of the number just before the point
    k = t - 1
    while k > 0 and s[k - 1].isdigit() and d[k - 1] == d[t]:
        k -= 1
    before = s[k - 1] if k > 0 and d[k - 1] == d[t] else ""
    # a point after a newline, colon or another point (versions, lists) is not a decimal point
    if before in (".", "\n", ":") or before.endswith("\n"):
        return None, 0.0
    digits = t - k
    value = LEAD_ZERO if s[k] == "0" else OTHER_DECIMAL
    if digits >= 3:
        value *= 0.5
    return None, value

"""Approximate a signed spelling-fragment feature, not a topic detector.

Strong positives are n-ad, n-ag and related short fragments; n-ew and
labial continuations are negative. The boundary matters: 'n' + 'ad'
and the short token 'nad' count, but a whole word like 'Canada' does not.
Cyrillic н-ад is stronger. A few weaker n-vowel continuations and small
first-token offsets are included. State is the preceding token plus an
escape flag; it resets at document boundaries.
"""
import re
from functools import lru_cache
from anyascii import anyascii

READS = ()

# Continuation after n; activation when split / in one short token.
FRAGMENTS = (
    (r'ad', 5.5, 6.3),
    (r'ad[ao]', 1.6, 0.0),
    (r'ad[eiyhsl]|ad[ei][a-z]{1,2}', 4.2, 0.0),
    (r'ag(?:[ahdn]|an)?', 4.4, 3.7),
    (r'ag[eo](?:[drs])?', 1.7, 0.0),
    (r'and', 3.9, 4.4),
    (r'anda', 6.9, 0.0),
    (r'and[a-z]{1,2}', 0.6, 0.0),
    (r'ath', 3.6, 3.4),
    (r'[au]j|azhd?', 2.1, 3.6),
    (r'ar|ah|ay|aud|ald', 0.8, 0.0),
    (r'ied[a-z]{0,2}', 0.4, 0.0),
    (r'nd|dh', 1.4, 0.0),
    (r'[eou]d[eoa]?', 0.4, 0.0),
    (r'ew', -5.4, 0.0),
    (r'ews', -2.9, 0.0),
    (r'[ao]v[aer]?|ow', -1.0, 0.0),
    (r'um(?:[sue]|ber)?', -1.9, 0.0),
    (r'em[ae]|amed', -0.7, 0.0),
)
PATTERNS = [(re.compile(p), a, b) for p, a, b in FRAGMENTS]
SYLLABLES = ((r'd|dh|ud', 0.4), (r'j[ie]?|zh|kh|f', 0.5),
             (r'v|w|um', -0.9), (r'ad', 3.7))


@lru_cache(maxsize=20000)
def roman(text):
    if text.isascii():
        return text.lower()
    # Keep these written letters explicit in the transliteration.
    text = text.replace('й', 'j').replace('Й', 'J').replace('ا', 'a')
    return anyascii(text).lower()


def spelling(previous, current):
    s = roman(current)
    split = (not current[:1].isspace() and
             previous[-1:].lower() in {'n', 'н', 'ñ', 'ν', 'ن'} and
             not previous.endswith(r'\n'))
    if not split and not current[:1].isspace():
        if re.search(r'n[aeiou]$', roman(previous)):
            for pattern, value in SYLLABLES:
                if re.fullmatch(pattern, s):
                    return value
    whole = s.strip()
    if split:
        tail = s
    elif whole.startswith('n') and len(whole) <= 5:
        tail = whole[1:]
    else:
        return 0.0
    for pattern, separate, together in PATTERNS:
        if not pattern.fullmatch(tail):
            continue
        cyrillic_ad = pattern.pattern == 'ad' and 'ад' in current.lower()
        value = separate if split else together
        if cyrillic_ad:
            value = 10.4 if split else 7.9
        if split:
            p = roman(previous).strip()
            if pattern.pattern == 'and' and p == 'n' and not current.isupper():
                return 0.0
            if len(p) > 5:
                value *= 0.25
            if cyrillic_ad and previous.endswith('Н'):
                value *= 1.25
            if previous.endswith('ñ'):
                value *= 0.1
        return value
    return 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    same = carry is not None and carry[0] == doc
    previous = carry[1] if same else ''
    current = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    value = spelling(previous, current)
    if not previous and not value:
        s = current.strip()
        value = (-0.37 if current.startswith('<|') else
                 -0.22 if s.isdigit() else
                 -0.31 if current[:1].isspace() and s.isalpha() else
                 -0.10 if s.isalpha() else -0.17)
    # Literal backslash-n is an escape, not a nasal spelling fragment.
    if same and carry[2]:
        value = 0.0
    escaped_n = previous.endswith('\\') and current == 'n'
    return (doc, current, escaped_n), float(value)

"""Layer-1 MLP neuron behind down_proj component 865, predicted from the text.

The component is one hidden neuron of layer 1's MLP (its input direction is almost
entirely that single neuron), so its activation is that neuron's value, scaled. It is
rare and spiky: about 0.07% of positions are large, and most of the variance sits in
those spikes. Simple text rules capture only a little of it, so this program is a
modest approximation, not a full explanation. It uses two rules:

1. Document starts. At the first token of a document (the first token of a row, or
   the first token of a new packed document within a row) the neuron sits at about
   -0.18: attention has no earlier context there.
2. Ad/ag fragments inside words. When a word is split into pieces and a later piece
   is a short letter fragment containing "ad" or "ag" (e.g. "Bhavn|ag|ri",
   "Fukun|aga", "Gran|ad|inas", "N|ade|zh"), the neuron is often strongly positive.
   Many such fragments are not, so this rule only gives a small average shift.

Everything else predicts 0.
"""

import re

READS = ()

DOC_START_VALUE = -0.18
AD_AG_VALUE = 0.16
AD_AG = re.compile(r"a[dg]")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tokens = prefix.token_strings
    documents = prefix.document_ids
    if prefix.position == 0 or documents[-1] != documents[-2]:
        return carry, DOC_START_VALUE
    current, previous = tokens[-1], tokens[-2]
    inside_word = current.isalpha() and previous.strip()[-1:].isalpha()
    if inside_word and AD_AG.search(current.lower()):
        return carry, AD_AG_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:866 -- the "h + rare letter" detector.

What it does: this component goes strongly negative on a short letter fragment that
completes an "h" digraph inside a word, most of all the letter y: "Thy", "phy" (in
"physics"/"photography"-like splits), "hy", "Staph|y|lococcus", "eth|y|lene", "Duch|y".
Weaker negatives come from the other rare letters v, j, q, g, w, f, x after an h
("h|v", "h|j"). Letters that commonly follow an h (a, e, i, o, r, t, ...) do nothing, and
whole words (" why", " hydro", " physical") do nothing: the effect is on fragments.
A few fragments after an h push the other way: "eth|ion", "ah|are".

How it is read: the program looks at the current token and the last character of the
token before it (within the same document). Nothing else.

Main cases, as activations:
  h + y (fragment, e.g. "y" after "ph"/"ch"/"sh"/"th"/"h")   about -4
  h + v, j, q                                               about -2.5
  h + g, w, f, x                                            about -1
  fragment "hy", "hx" (no leading space)                     about -4
  same with a leading space (" hy", " thy", " shy")         about 0.7 x the above
  h + "ion", "are", "ire", "io" (positive)                  about +2 to +3
"""

READS = ()

# letter that follows an "h" inside a word -> activation
RARE_AFTER_H = {"y": -4.0, "v": -2.5, "j": -2.5, "q": -2.5, "g": -1.5, "w": -1.0, "f": -1.0, "x": -1.0}
# whole fragments after an "h" that push the component positive
AFTER_H_POSITIVE = {"ion": 3.0, "are": 3.0, "ire": 3.0, "io": 2.0, "ares": 1.5, "ac": 1.5}
SPACE_SCALE = 0.7  # a leading space (a word-initial fragment) weakens the effect


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2][-1:].lower() if same_doc else ""
    core = cur.strip().lower()
    if not (core.isascii() and core.isalpha()):
        return carry, 0.0
    if prev == "h" and not cur.startswith(" ") and core in AFTER_H_POSITIVE:
        return carry, AFTER_H_POSITIVE[core]
    if len(core) > 2:
        return carry, 0.0
    text = core if cur.startswith(" ") else prev + core
    value = 0.0
    for i in range(1, len(text)):
        if text[i - 1] == "h":
            v = RARE_AFTER_H.get(text[i], 0.0)
            if cur.startswith(" "):
                v *= SPACE_SCALE
            value = min(value, v)
    return carry, value

"""Approximate a local English possessive-phrase response.

Keep eight tokens after my/your/etc. or a genitive ending. Score selected
noun classes and their complement prepositions; distinguish the first
phrase word from later ones. Negative complement scores approximate the
strongest recurring pattern in the supplied examples. WordNet supplies
lemmas, feelings, kinship and peer categories.

Separate rules cover copulas, temporal/capitalized relational modifiers,
positive by/between/below continuations, and the colon of an initial Title:.
Other positions are near zero. Reset state between documents; distant and
most token-specific variation are intentionally not modeled.
"""
import re
from functools import lru_cache
import wordnet

READS = ()
POSSESSIVES = set('my your his her its our their whose'.split())
CONTRACTIONS = set('it he she that what who where there here let how when'.split())
PREPOSITIONS = set('of to in on as with for from at by about into over under '
                   'through between against without upon within toward towards '
                   'regarding below'.split())
COPULAS = set('is are was were be been being'.split())
BREAK_WORDS = set('a an the this that these those which who what not can could '
                  'will would shall should may might must do does did have has '
                  'had'.split())
# These are semantic/grammatical classes, not token IDs or individual scores.
NOUN_CLASSES = {
    'knowing': set('knowledge understanding comprehension awareness grasp '
                   'appreciation'.split()),
    'opinion': set('opinion view thought impression belief judgment perception'.split()),
    'assessment': set('assessment review examination evaluation analysis '
                      'interpretation calculation diagnosis'.split()),
    'connection': set('relationship connection interaction association involvement '
                      'participation influence impact reaction response'.split()),
    'role': set('role position importance significance place status reputation'.split()),
    'commitment': set('commitment dedication duty responsibility contribution '
                      'devotion loyalty allegiance obligation'.split()),
    'capacity': set('ability inability skill talent strength weakness potential '
                    'capability capacity'.split()),
    'experience': set('career tenure debut journey travel experience performance '
                      'repertoire'.split()),
    'aim': set('desire need goal plan dream interest intention purpose aspiration '
               'willingness reluctance'.split()),
    'identity': {'self', 'selves'},
    'home': {'home', 'hometown'},
    'work': set('work research study service employment practice'.split()),
    'representation': set('portrayal description depiction disclosure representation '
                          'presentation expression'.split()),
}
COMPLEMENTS = {
    'knowing': {'of', 'about'},
    'opinion': {'on', 'of', 'about', 'regarding', 'toward', 'towards'},
    'assessment': {'of', 'on'},
    'connection': {'to', 'with', 'on', 'in', 'between'},
    'role': {'in', 'as', 'on', 'of'},
    'commitment': {'to', 'of', 'for', 'toward', 'towards'},
    'capacity': {'to', 'for', 'of'},
    'experience': {'in', 'of', 'as', 'with', 'on', 'at'},
    'aim': {'to', 'for', 'of', 'in'},
    'work': {'on', 'in', 'of', 'with', 'for'},
    'representation': {'of', 'on'},
    'emotion': {'for', 'about', 'toward', 'towards', 'on'},
}
# Scores for the noun directly after the possessive, a later noun,
# and its complement preposition, respectively.
LEVELS = {
    'aim': (-0.25, -0.29, -0.29),
    'assessment': (-0.08, -0.03, -0.78),
    'capacity': (-0.33, -0.41, -0.53),
    'commitment': (-0.39, -0.33, -0.59),
    'connection': (-0.1, -0.08, -0.55),
    'emotion': (-0.08, -0.07, -0.43),
    'experience': (-0.39, -0.46, -0.29),
    'family': (-0.04, -0.15, 0.001),
    'home': (-0.24, -0.33, 0.001),
    'identity': (-0.2, -0.75, 0.001),
    'knowing': (-0.11, -0.16, -0.96),
    'opinion': (-0.17, -0.18, -0.7),
    'peers': (-0.14, -0.3, 0.001),
    'representation': (0.001, 0.001, -0.33),
    'role': (-0.21, -0.16, -0.61),
    'work': (-0.19, -0.09, -0.29),
}
SPECIAL = {
    'background': 0.0015,
    'capitalized_relational_modifier': 0.1821,
    'copula': -0.0955,
    'temporal_modifier': -0.2224,
    'title_colon': -2.981,
}
CONTINUATIONS = {
    'below': 0.27,
    'between': 0.39,
    'by': 0.3,
}

@lru_cache(maxsize=16000)
def noun_class(word):
    forms = {word, *wordnet.base_forms(word)}
    for name, nouns in NOUN_CLASSES.items():
        if nouns & forms:
            return name
    if any(wordnet.is_a(word, root) for root in
           ('friend', 'colleague', 'peer', 'counterpart', 'ally',
            'enemy', 'teammate', 'companion')):
        return 'peers'
    if 'noun.feeling' in wordnet.categories(word):
        return 'emotion'
    if wordnet.is_a(word, 'relative'):
        return 'family'
    return None


def advance(carry, token, doc):
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        carry = (doc, '', 99, '', '', 0)
    _, phrase, age, previous, first, position = carry
    word = token.strip().lower()
    starts_word = (bool(token[:1].isspace()) or position == 0
                   or (word in POSSESSIVES and token[:1].isupper()))
    label = 'background'
    if position == 1 and first == 'Title' and token == ':':
        label = 'title_colon'
    elif age < 8:
        phrase += token
        words = re.findall(r'[a-zA-Z]+', phrase.lower())
        blocked = any(w in PREPOSITIONS | COPULAS | BREAK_WORDS for w in words[:-1])
        if words and not blocked and token.strip() and token.strip()[-1].isalpha():
            current = words[-1]
            n = len(words)
            if current in PREPOSITIONS and n >= 2:
                head = noun_class(words[-2])
                if current in COMPLEMENTS.get(head, ()):
                    label = ('complement', head)
                elif current in {'by', 'between', 'below'}:
                    label = ('continuation', current)
            elif current in COPULAS and n >= 2:
                label = 'copula'
            elif current not in BREAK_WORDS | POSSESSIVES | PREPOSITIONS | {'and', 'or'}:
                kind = noun_class(current)
                bucket = 'direct' if n == 1 else 'modified'
                if kind:
                    label = (kind, bucket)
                elif current in {'past', 'previous', 'former', 'prior'}:
                    label = 'temporal_modifier'
                elif token.strip()[:1].isupper() and 'adj.pert' in wordnet.categories(current):
                    label = 'capitalized_relational_modifier'
        if re.search(r'[,.!?;:\n]', token):
            age = 99
        else:
            age += 1
    genitive = token in ("'s", '’s') and previous not in CONTRACTIONS
    plural_genitive = token in ("'", '’') and previous.endswith('s')
    if (word in POSSESSIVES and starts_word) or genitive or plural_genitive:
        phrase, age = '', 0
    if position == 0:
        first = token
    if word:
        previous = word if starts_word else previous + word
    return (doc, phrase[-100:], age, previous[-40:], first, position + 1), label


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    carry, label = advance(carry, prefix.token_strings[-1], prefix.document_ids[-1])
    if isinstance(label, str):
        value = SPECIAL.get(label, 0.001)
    elif label[0] == 'complement':
        value = LEVELS[label[1]][2]
    elif label[0] == 'continuation':
        value = CONTINUATIONS[label[1]]
    else:
        value = LEVELS.get(label[0], (0.001, 0.001))[label[1] == 'modified']
    return carry, value

noun that wants a following complement: "his career", "her debut", "my friends",
"their abilities", "his tenure", "our understanding" (then "of", "in", "to"...).
The step predicts:
  - a relational noun right after a possessive (my/his/her/their/its/your/our): -0.3
  - a relational noun anywhere else: -0.1
  - a preposition directly after a relational noun ("understanding of", "role in"): -0.15
  - everything else: 0

POSSESSIVES = {"my", "his", "her", "their", "its", "your", "our"}
PREPOSITIONS = {"of", "to", "in", "on", "with", "as", "for", "by", "at", "from", "between"}
RELATIONAL_NOUNS = {
    # people and relationships
    "friend", "friends", "cousin", "uncle", "husband", "wife", "colleague", "colleagues",
    "counterpart", "counterparts", "ally", "allies", "comrades", "predecessor", "associates",
    "ancestors", "relatives", "peers",
    # careers, roles and duties
    "career", "debut", "tenure", "duty", "duties", "obligations", "role", "roles",
    "position", "quest", "plans", "goals", "travels", "contribution", "commitment",
    "commitments", "influence", "impact", "view", "views", "interest", "interests",
    # abilities and knowledge
    "ability", "abilities", "skills", "skill", "understanding", "knowledge", "experience",
    "capacity", "expertise", "talents", "intake",

def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()

    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if same_doc else ""

"""Layer-1 MLP down_proj component 868, a sparse "negative on word-continuation pieces" feature.

What it does, in plain terms:
  1. Chat role name: the word "user" right after the chat marker "<|im_start|>" gets a
     strong negative value (about -1).
  2. Split words: a token made only of ASCII letters, with no leading space, that follows
     another letter-only piece of at least two letters (e.g. "myn" then "umber" in
     "mynumber", "fint" then "ype") is a continuation of a word split across tokens. It
     gets a small negative value (about -0.05), made more negative (up to about -0.25)
     when the surrounding text is code-like, judged by a running density of code
     punctuation ({}();=_<>[]/\\) that resets at each document boundary.
  3. Everything else is 0.

Why: the component is mostly silent and fires negatively on the later pieces of
identifiers and words split into tokens, most strongly in code. Simple rules capture
only part of it: the largest spikes (down to about -10) depend on context a short
rule cannot see.
"""
READS = ()
CODE_MARKS = set("{}();=_<>[]/\\")


def _letters(s):
    return len(s) > 0 and all(c.isascii() and c.isalpha() for c in s)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    s = prefix.token_strings
    t = len(s) - 1
    new_doc = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    density = 0.0 if (carry is None or new_doc) else carry
    is_code = any(c in CODE_MARKS for c in s[-1])
    density = 0.95 * density + 0.05 * (1.0 if is_code else 0.0)
    if t >= 1 and s[-1] == "user" and s[-2] == "<|im_start|>":
        value = -1.0
    elif t >= 1 and _letters(s[-1]) and _letters(s[-2]) and len(s[-2]) >= 2 and not s[-1].startswith(" "):
        value = -0.05 - 0.2 * density
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return density, value

"""Document-opening tokens: the first token of each document.

What it does, in plain terms
----------------------------
This component is almost silent everywhere except on the first token of a
document. That token has no earlier text in its document (the model resets
attention at each document boundary), so the component's value there depends
only on which token it is, and it is large: roughly -23 to +11. At every other
position its activation is within about +/-0.2, so the program predicts 0 there.

At a document's first token the program predicts a value from the token's kind:

* indentation (a tab, or 3+ spaces, no newline)            -> negative
    (a tab or 5+ spaces: about -12 to -15; 3-4 spaces: about -4)
* connectives and clause linkers that need earlier text to
  make sense, capitalised at the start (And, But, So,
  However, Thus, Wait, ...)                                  -> strongly negative (-9)
* the same kind of linker mid-sentence, with a leading
  space (and, or, that, if, this, but, so, ...), and the
  weaker openers This/They/If/That                          -> negative (-4.5)
* code keywords (null, true, false, var, else, return, ...) -> negative (-8)
* capitalised openers that can start a text on their own
  (The, In, We, How, I, An, By, When, There, It, ...)
  and single capital letters (A, R, C, ...)                 -> positive (+4)
* auxiliary verbs (is, was, are, were, be, been)            -> positive (+4)
* other function words (the, a, of, in, on, at, for, ...)   -> mildly positive (+2)
* markup and comment openers (#, /*, //, **, [, $, __, ...)
  with no letters and no leading space                       -> positive (+4)
* everything else                                            -> 0

Values are tuned on about 98,000 document-opening tokens from the training data.
A full per-token table would score higher, but it is a list of token ids with no concept behind it.
"""

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

TAB_INDENT = -12.0
LONG_SPACES = -15.0
MID_SPACES = -4.0
CODE_KEYWORD = -8.0
CAPITAL_LINKER = -9.0
LINKER = -4.5
CAPITAL_OPENER = 4.0
AUXILIARY = 4.0
FUNCTION_WORD = 2.0
MARKUP_OPENER = 4.0

# Connectives and clause linkers: they presuppose earlier text.
LINKERS = set(
    "and or but so if that this they however therefore thus then now here even "
    "maybe perhaps while though although because since yet still actually basically "
    "ultimately later earlier hmm oh ah yes well wait hey hi sorry like today "
    "recently sure".split()
)
# Words that are weaker openers when capitalised, so they stay in the mild tier.
WEAK_CAPITAL_LINKERS = set("This They If That Today Here".split())
CODE_KEYWORDS = set(
    "null nil true false var let val void return else elif elsif bool boolean "
    "nullptr new goto throw catch".split()
)
# Capitalised words that can open a text by themselves.
OPENERS = set("The In We How I An By When There It What Which".split())
AUXILIARIES = set("is was are were be been".split())
FUNCTION_WORDS = set("the a an of in on at by from with for not have has".split())
MARKUP_STARTS = ("#", "/*", "//", "**", "[", "$", "-", "_", "\\", "<?")


def value_of(token: str) -> float:
    """The predicted activation for a document's first token, given its string."""
    if token.strip() == "":
        if "\n" in token:
            return 0.0
        if "\t" in token:
            return TAB_INDENT
        if len(token) >= 5:
            return LONG_SPACES
        if len(token) >= 3:
            return MID_SPACES
        return 0.0
    word = token.strip()
    lower = word.lower()
    leading_space = token[0].isspace()
    capitalised = word[0].isupper() and not leading_space
    if word in CODE_KEYWORDS or lower in CODE_KEYWORDS:
        return CODE_KEYWORD
    if lower in LINKERS:
        if capitalised and word not in WEAK_CAPITAL_LINKERS:
            return CAPITAL_LINKER
        return LINKER
    if capitalised and word in OPENERS:
        return CAPITAL_OPENER
    if not leading_space and len(word) == 1 and word.isupper():
        return CAPITAL_OPENER
    if lower in AUXILIARIES:
        return AUXILIARY
    if lower in FUNCTION_WORDS:
        return FUNCTION_WORD

   "author of" (about -7.5 on average); creative-work roles are stronger than

counts at the token that completes it.

    "author": -7.5, "creator": -4.0, "authors": -3.0, "creators": -3.0,

    "recipient": -1.1, "chairman": -1.0, "host": -1.0, "artist": -1.0,
    "producer": -1.0, "publisher": -1.0, "director": -0.8, "professor": -0.7,
    "manager": -0.7,
}

# completed character or word -> the component's activation on it
CREDIT_WORDS = {
    "摂": -10.0, "摄": -8.0, "攝": -8.0, "撮": -5.0,
    "撰": -4.0, "著作": -4.0, "撰写": -3.0, "主持": -3.0, "摄影": -3.0, "撮影": -3.0,
    "著": -1.0, "影": -1.0, "製": -2.0, "植": -2.0, "氏": -2.0, "演": -1.0,
    "저": -2.0, "작": -2.0,
}

    t = prefix.position

"""Negative spelling responses, especially short stem + suffix continuations.

Follow the current Latin-letter word through token pieces. Recognize families
such as importance, proportion, dominance, coordination, abundance, and orbit.
Give larger negative pulses when a short or-/ord-/und-/bin- fragment is joined
to its continuation. These are spelling rules, not a general semantic test.
Other scripts and most fine contextual variation are left unexplained.
"""
import re

READS = ()

# Related word forms share one stem; larger magnitudes mark stronger families.
FAMILIES = (
    (r'importan', -0.4),
    (r'importance', -1.2),
    (r'proport', -1.4),
    (r'disproport', -2.4),
    (r'domina', -1.5),
    (r'dominan', -2.5),
    (r'prominen', -0.8),
    (r'correspond', -0.6),
    (r'ordin(?:at|an)', -0.7),
    (r'(?:ab|red)undan', -1.7),
    (r'compound', -0.7),
    (r'compounded', -2.3),
    (r'recombin', -1.8),
    (r'determinant', -0.7),
    (r'ou?rb[io]', -1.8),
    (r'ordon', -2.0),
    (r'ordonn', -5.5),
    (r'ordn', -4.5),
)
FAMILIES = tuple((re.compile(p), v) for p, v in FAMILIES)
WORD_END = re.compile(r'[a-z]+$')
SHORT_OR = re.compile(r'\s*[a-z]{0,2}ou?r$')
SHORT_ORD = re.compile(r'\s*(?:[a-z]{0,2}ord|(?:ac|con|dis)cord)$')
SHORT_NASAL = re.compile(r'\s*(?:[a-z]?und|bin)$')


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    start = carry is None or carry[0] != doc
    old, previous = ('', '') if start else carry[1:]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1].lower()
    continuation = bool(old and token and token[0].isalpha())
    text = (old if continuation else '') + token
    match = WORD_END.search(text)
    word = match.group()[-80:] if match else ''

    value = 0.0
    # 'forbid' contains the letters orbi but is not part of the orbit family.
    for pattern, strength in FAMILIES:
        if pattern.search(word) and not word.startswith('forbid'):
            value = min(value, strength)

    if continuation:
        if (SHORT_OR.fullmatch(previous) and previous.strip() != 'for'
                and re.match(r'(?:b[io]|dn|mon|ton)', token)):
            value = min(value, -4.0)
        if (SHORT_ORD.fullmatch(previous)
                and re.match(r'(?:an(?:ce|t)|onn|inate)', token)):
            value = min(value, -5.0)
        if SHORT_NASAL.fullmatch(previous) and token.startswith(('ant', 'ance')):
            value = min(value, -4.0)
        if previous.endswith('orb') and token.startswith('ance'):
            value = min(value, -3.5)
        if token.startswith('ordon'):
            value = min(value, -4.0)

    return (doc, word, token), value + (0.21 if start else 0.0)

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:872: a "Latin o-cluster inside a split word" detector.

What it does. Most of the time this component is silent (about 0). It goes negative on
the later pieces of a word that the tokenizer split into several tokens (the pieces after
the first one, with no space in front), when the letters of the word so far contain an
"o + r/n/d/b" cluster. The strongest clusters are "orb" and "bon"; "ord", "omb", "onn",
"ond", "pon", "ound", "ina", "port" and "ance" are medium; "ort", "rd", "ant", "dn" are weak.
Examples it responds to: ordon|nance, sor|bit|ol, coord|in|ates, Or|dn|ung,
recomb|in|ant, im|port|ance, comor|bid|ities.
It also reads a small positive value (+0.2) on the first token of each document, where
the attention context resets; there the component averages about +0.2.

Why. The clusters are letter patterns a person can read; the program is a lexical
approximation of the component, not a copy of the model's computation. Strength is
additive over the clusters present in the word.

What it misses. Sign and size depend on context the letters alone do not show: "ates"
is strongly negative in coördinates but near 0 in skates; some large positive peaks on
ordinary continuation pieces are not captured. Word-initial tokens are not predicted
(including them makes the fit worse).
"""
READS = ()

CLUSTERS = {
    "orb": -1.0, "bon": -0.5, "ord": -0.4, "omb": -0.4, "pom": -0.2,
    "onn": -0.2, "ond": -0.2, "pon": -0.2, "ound": -0.2, "ina": -0.2,
    "port": -0.2, "ance": -0.2, "ort": -0.1, "rd": -0.1, "ant": -0.1, "dn": -0.1,
}
DOC_START = 0.2


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """carry: the current word's letters so far, lowercase ('' outside a word)."""
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        return tok.strip().lower(), DOC_START
    letters = tok.strip().replace("'", "").isalpha()
    # a continuation piece: letters, no leading space, and the previous piece was a word piece
    continues = letters and not tok[:1].isspace() and bool(carry)
    if not continues:
        return (tok.strip().lower() if letters else ""), 0.0
    word = carry + tok.lower()
    return word, sum((weight for cluster, weight in CLUSTERS.items() if cluster in word), 0.0)

' [' immediately afterward gets a smaller one. Otherwise use a negative
first-token baseline and zero later. This omits small token-specific signals.

"""Layer 1 MLP down-projection, component 873: two readable triggers.

1. The colon of a document-opening "Title:" label: the word "Title" that starts a
   document (right after <|endoftext|>, or at the start of a row), followed by ":".
   This is the component's only large response, about +6.8.
2. The filler token "··" (a run of middle dots): about -1.0.

Everywhere else it predicts 0. The first token of each document segment has a mean
of about -0.24, but predicting that offset made the model's predictions worse, so it is
left out.
"""

READS = ()

TITLE_COLON = 6.78
DOT_FILLER = -0.97
END_OF_TEXT = "<|endoftext|>"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    strings = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    t = prefix.position
    here = strings[-1]
    if here == "··":
        return carry, DOT_FILLER
    if t >= 1 and here == ":" and strings[-2] == "Title":
        i = t - 1  # position of "Title"
        starts_doc = i == 0 or docs[i] != docs[i - 1] or strings[i - 1] == END_OF_TEXT
        if starts_doc:
            return carry, TITLE_COLON

"""Layer 1 MLP down_proj, component 874: a "p-e spelling" detector.

In plain terms, this component goes negative when the model is reading the
letters "p" and "e" in a word fragment, and it stays near zero elsewhere:

1. Short fragments that start with "pe": "pe", "pes", "ped", "pen", "pet",
   "pec", "peg" (strongest: about -2 on average, up to -8 in rare words such
   as "Vieillespes|se"). The common word "per" is excluded: it is ~0.
2. A few "pi" words that are whole word pieces: "pie", "piece", "pieces",
   "pick", "picked", "picks" (about -1.9). Other "pi"/"pe" starts are weak
   (about -0.3).
3. An "e" that completes a "p" + "e" pair split across two tokens, with no
   space before it: the "e" of "Hep|es", "P|ec|let", "логоп|ед", "π|ε"
   (about -1.2; about -2 when the "p" is Cyrillic п or Greek π).

The program predicts these typical sizes and 0 everywhere else. It only reads
the current token and the one before it, within the same document.
"""

READS = ()

# Whole words beginning "pi" that the component also responds to.
PI_WORDS = {"pie", "pieces", "piece", "pick", "picked", "picks"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    raw = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    tok = raw.strip().lower()
    same_doc = len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_doc else ""

    # 1. Short "pe" fragments; "per" is a common whole word and does not count.
    if tok.startswith("pe") and len(tok) <= 3 and tok != "per":
        return carry, -1.9
    # 2. "pi" words that are whole word pieces.
    if tok in PI_WORDS:
        return carry, -1.9
    # Other words starting "pe"/"pi" (short, not "per"): weak.
    if tok.startswith(("pe", "pi")) and len(tok) <= 5 and not tok.startswith("per"):
        return carry, -0.3
    # 3. An "e" (or Cyrillic/Greek equivalent) directly after a "p" ending the previous token.
    if prev.endswith(("p", "π", "п")) and not raw.startswith(" ") and tok[:1] in ("e", "é", "ε", "е"):

    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer-1 MLP down_proj component 876: a sparse detector with three parts.

1. Negative on the lone space that begins a line of a line-numbered listing (`cat -n`
   output such as '    96\\t...'), just before the line number. Strongly negative.
2. Positive on the lone lead byte 0xC2 of a two-byte UTF-8 character (token 126; the
   start of, e.g., a non-breaking space). Strongly positive.
3. Weaker positive values on code-ish tokens: '::' (Rust/C++ paths), backticks, middle-dot
   indent runs, source-file extensions such as '.go' and '.rs', and a '2' glued to a word
   (sqlite2, VARCHAR2, vec2). Everything else is 0.

curve, so the program stays readable.

import re

READS = ()

NUMBERED_LINE = re.compile(r"\s*\d+\t")
LEAD_BYTE_C2 = 126
CODE_TOKENS = {"::": 0.6, "`": 0.45, " `": 0.38, "··": 0.47}
SOURCE_EXTENSIONS = {".go", ".rs", ".ts", ".py", ".mod"}
WORD_END = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z]$")


def in_numbered_listing(prefix):
    """True when the line above the current (space-only) line is a numbered `cat -n` line."""
    lines = prefix.text_prefixes[prefix.position].split("\n")
    return len(lines) >= 2 and bool(NUMBERED_LINE.match(lines[-2]))


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if token == " " and in_numbered_listing(prefix):
        return carry, -0.67
    if prefix.token_ids[-1] == LEAD_BYTE_C2:
        return carry, 1.7
    if token in CODE_TOKENS:

    if token in SOURCE_EXTENSIONS:
        return carry, 0.4
    if token == "2" and len(prefix) > 1 and WORD_END.search(prefix.token_strings[-2]):
        return carry, 0.2
    return carry, 0.0

The listed words concern duration, age, difficulty, prohibition and manner.
Traditional spellings are simplified; a leading 的 is ignored for matching.

0.06. A negative onset correction depends on script, letters and spaces.
Other tokens get zero. This omits many weaker token-specific responses.
